question: Will God flood the earth again?
summary: Genesis 9:11-15 gives an unqualified covenantal 'no' — God swears never again to flood the earth, with the rainbow as the binding sign. Nahum 1:8, however, describes God using 'an overrunning flood' to make an utter end of his enemies' place.

reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish scope and sense: Genesis forbids only another universal water-deluge, while Nahum's "flood" is a local, figurative judgment on one city.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (Steve Wells) presses the objection directly, reading Nahum 1:8's "overrunning flood" as God again destroying everything by water against the Genesis 9 promise.

pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats both passages directly: the Genesis promise excludes only a general deluge (allowing particular inundations), and Nahum's flood is the Medo-Babylonian army 'like a flood' (or the literal river breach) against Nineveh alone.

excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly limits the Gen 9 promise to a universal deluge, explicitly allowing local inundations — the core scope harmonization against Nahum's local flood.
excerpts.source_note_text:
And I will establish my covenant with you,.... This is repeated to denote the certainty of it, as well as to lead on to the particulars of it:
neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters of a flood; neither man nor beast, at least not all of them, and especially by water:
neither shall there be any more a flood to destroy the earth; not a general deluge, otherwise notwithstanding this promise there might be, as there have been, particular inundations, which have overflowed particular countries and places, but not the whole earth; and this hinders not but that the whole earth may be destroyed by fire, as it will be at the last day, only not by water any more; and this is the sum and substance of the covenant with Noah, his sons, and all the creatures that have been, or shall be.
